summary:
Earth Jukebox: Listen to a Changing Planet

Earth Jukebox is a website that turns NASA Earth data into music. It covers global temperature, CO₂, Arctic sea ice, sea level and ocean heat, plus NASA POWER climate records for 86 places around the world. Each data point becomes a note, so a rising temperature becomes a melody that climbs higher. Visitors can spin a realistic 3D globe, tap a city to hear its climate, see temperature, rain and wind data maps, and play all the datasets together as an “orchestra”. Live graphs and a sound spectrum play alongside the music, so you can see and hear the data at once.

Sparky is an animated AI guide that greets visitors and answers questions by text or voice. It explains things at a kids’ level or a grown-up level.

Charts can feel abstract and hard to approach. Sound makes climate change something you can feel, and it opens NASA data to people who are blind or have low vision. Captions, keyboard controls and reduced-motion settings make the site inclusive. Earth Jukebox helps people of every age understand our changing planet and care about it.
details:
Earth Jukebox turns NASA Earth data into music. It covers global temperature, CO₂, Arctic sea ice, sea level, ocean heat, and climate records for 86 places from NASA POWER. Each measurement is mapped to a note, so a rising value makes the melody climb. Visitors can spin a 3D Earth, tap a place to hear its climate, view temperature, rain, and wind data maps, and play the datasets together as an “orchestra.” Live graphs and a sound spectrum run alongside the audio, so people can see and hear the same numbers.

Sparky, an animated guide, greets visitors by time of day, asks whether they are a kid or a grown-up, and explains things at that level. Visitors can type or speak their questions. Common questions get instant answers from built-in notes, and other questions go to an AI server with caching and rate-limit handling.

It makes abstract climate trends easy to feel as well as see. It opens NASA data to people who are blind or have low vision, because the sound carries the information. It offers two explanation levels, for kids and for grown-ups. It runs in any modern browser with nothing to install, and it includes captions, keyboard controls, and a reduce-motion setting.

The aim is to help people of all ages notice and care about how the planet is changing. It also gives teachers and science communicators a new way to present NASA data.

Tools: JavaScript (ES modules), HTML, CSS, and Python for the local server, build script, and data processing. three.js 0.170 with custom shaders for the globe, clouds, atmosphere, and data layers. Web Audio API for sonification, Web Speech API for microphone input, and Cartesia text-to-speech for Sparky’s voice. NASA POWER climatology for the 86 places. A Cloudflare Worker serves Sparky’s AI answers. Built and tested on a Windows 11 PC.

Accessibility: captions, screen-reader value announcements, high-contrast mode, and reduced motion. Age range: separate explanations for kids and grown-ups. Cost and limits: an answer cache, instant local answers, and handling for the AI server’s limit of 10 questions per minute. Privacy: no API keys are embedded in the page, and location is used only when a visitor presses “Near me.”

Team: Arshal Aromal (backend developer and team lead), Adarsh S (UI/UX lead and bug testing), Nevin Biju Samuel (UI/UX design and backend debugging), Harigovind (information research and advising), Arundhathi Asok (PowerPoint and information organizing), and Aishwariya Santhosh (PowerPoint and idea pitching).
